/**
 * Shared vocabulary for the app's view transitions.
 *
 * Three things have to agree for a transition to work, so they live together
 * here: the `<ViewTransition name>` that pairs two elements, the transition
 * types that `<Link>` announces, and the View Transition Class names that
 * `app/globals.css` styles.
 */

/**
 * Names the shared element that morphs between the grid thumbnail and the
 * detail hero. React requires `name` to be unique among all *mounted*
 * `<ViewTransition>` components, so it is namespaced by slug: the grid has four
 * of these on screen at once, and only the one matching the destination hero
 * forms a pair.
 */
export function productImageTransitionName(slug: string): string {
  return `product-image-${slug}`
}

/** Navigating deeper into the app: grid → product detail. */
export const NAV_FORWARD = 'nav-forward'

/** Navigating back out: product detail → grid. */
export const NAV_BACK = 'nav-back'

/**
 * Page-level transition props for the grid, which sits "outside" the detail
 * page: it leaves to the left on the way in and returns from the left.
 *
 * `default: 'none'` switches every trigger off except the ones listed below, so
 * the wrapper only animates on a real navigation — never on an unrelated
 * re-render — and untyped navigations (e.g. a bare `router.push`) stay still
 * instead of animating in an arbitrary direction.
 */
export const gridPageTransition = {
  default: 'none',
  exit: { [NAV_FORWARD]: 'vt-slide-out-left', default: 'none' },
  enter: { [NAV_BACK]: 'vt-slide-in-left', default: 'none' },
} as const

/** The mirror image of {@link gridPageTransition}, for the detail page. */
export const detailPageTransition = {
  default: 'none',
  enter: { [NAV_FORWARD]: 'vt-slide-in-right', default: 'none' },
  exit: { [NAV_BACK]: 'vt-slide-out-right', default: 'none' },
} as const

/**
 * Props for the grid thumbnail / detail hero pair.
 *
 * `default: 'none'` is load-bearing: it keeps the `view-transition-name` off the
 * element unless this particular image is actually paired with its counterpart.
 * Without it the three thumbnails that *don't* match the destination would each
 * be snapshotted into their own group and animate independently of the page
 * slide, instead of travelling with it.
 */
export const sharedProductImage = {
  default: 'none',
  share: 'vt-product-image',
} as const

 * reveal an "update": the box morphs from skeleton height to content height
 * while the two cross-fade, rather than hard-swapping.
 */
export const suspenseReveal = {
  default: 'none',
  update: 'vt-reveal',
} as const

Done. All four behaviors are implemented and verified in a real browser.

## What I built

**`lib/view-transitions.ts`** (new) — one place holding the three things that have to agree: the `ViewTransition` names that pair elements, the transition types `<Link>` announces, and the CSS class names `globals.css` styles.

**Shared element morph** — the grid thumbnail and detail hero both get `name={`product-image-${slug}`}`, so React pairs them into a share transition. The key detail is `default: 'none'` alongside `share`: it keeps the `view-transition-name` off unless an image is *actually* paired. Without it, the three thumbnails that don't match the destination would each snapshot into their own group and animate independently instead of travelling with the page slide. I confirmed this in React's source (`react-dom-client.development.js:14494`) — when the class resolves to `"none"`, React skips applying a name entirely.

**Directional slides** — `<Link transitionTypes={['nav-forward']}>` on cards, `['nav-back']` on the back link; each page's `ViewTransition` maps those types to slide classes, mirrored so back is the reverse of forward.

**Suspense reveal** — the `ViewTransition` wraps the boundary rather than each branch, so skeleton and content share one name and the reveal is an "update": the box morphs from skeleton height to content height while the two cross-fade. On the detail page the hero is deliberately kept *outside* the boundary, since a shared element can't pair with a counterpart still behind a fallback.

**Reduced motion** — every rule that produces movement lives in `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference)`. The `reduce` block kills all group animations (geometry snaps, so nothing travels or resizes) and leaves a 120ms opacity cross-fade. It uses universal selectors so the browser's own `root` transition is covered too, and it also stops the pre-existing skeleton pulse.

No `next.config.ts` change: Next 16.4 no longer gates view transitions behind an experimental flag. `<ViewTransition>` works directly in these Server Components — Next's vendored react-server build exports it and the flight serializer supports it.

## Verification

Built, typechecked, then drove it in headless Chromium, instrumenting `document.startViewTransition` to capture the animations that actually ran:

- **Forward:** 2 transitions. First: hero morph at 420ms + old page `vt-exit-left` + new page `vt-enter-right`, with exactly **one** image named. Second (the Suspense reveal): `vt-fade-out` → `vt-reveal-in` on `.product-info`.
- **Back:** directions correctly reversed (`vt-exit-right` / `vt-enter-left`).
- **Reduced motion:** zero group animations, no slide keyframes anywhere, only 120ms fades — including on `root`. Skeleton pulse `animationName: none`.
- Probed computed styles mid-morph: old and new snapshots are geometrically identical (439.5×422.1px, `object-fit: cover`), so they coincide exactly. Mid-transition screenshots show the morph, the slide, and unpaired thumbnails moving with the page.

## Two things worth knowing

- **The browser back button doesn't animate** — I measured zero transitions started on `goBack()`. React skips view transitions on `popstate`; only the in-app back link animates. Fixing that needs router-level Navigation API support, not something I can do from app code.
- **Pre-existing, left alone:** the detail page renders a bare `<div>` while the home page uses `<main>`, so it doesn't pick up the `max-width`/`padding` from `main` and sits flush to the viewport edge. That makes the two pages slide at slightly different insets. Changing it would alter your existing layout, so I didn't — say the word and it's a one-line fix.

For verification I installed Playwright and Chromium under `/tmp/vtcheck` and, via `sudo dnf`, the system libraries Chromium needs (`nspr`, `nss`, etc.). Nothing was added to your project's dependencies, and I removed the `.next` build output, `next-env.d.ts`, and the tsconfig reformatting that `next build` introduced.
